title: The Science of Badminton: Game Characteristics, Anthropometry, Physiology, Visual Fitness and Biomechanics
author: Phomsoupha M, Laffaye G
notes: Typical rally 7 s / rest 15 s / effective playing time 31%; ~60-70% aerobic and ~30% anaerobic energy, mainly alactic rather than lactic; mean HR >90% HRmax; mean match lactate 4.4 mmol/L (range 2.9-12.2); matches 40 min-1 h; lunges ~17.9% of singles movements; sweat rate 1.11 L/h; aerobic capacity aids recovery between rallies; VO2max ~56 (men) / ~47 (women) ml/kg/min.

title: Physiological characteristics of badminton match play
author: Faude O, Meyer T, Rosenberger F, Fries M, Huber G, Kindermann W
notes: 12 international players, simulated match: rally 5.5 s, rest 11.4 s, 5.1 shots/rally; VO2 73% of peak; HR 89% of peak; lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Conclusion: both alactic anaerobic and aerobic energy are important; good aerobic endurance needed for fast recovery between rallies and for intensive training. DOI 10.1007/s00421-007-0441-8.

title: Match-play data according to playing categories in badminton: a systematic review
author: Winata B, Brochhagen J, Apriantono T, Hoppe MW
publisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 7
notes: Pooled values by category: MS rally 8.8 s / rest 22.9 s; WS 9.3 / 17.2 s; MD 6.5 / 24.9 s; rest between games ~134-147 s; work density ~0.4 singles; avg HR 163-169 bpm; one study 160-240 lunges per men's singles match (mean 194). Almost all data from elite players; only one study on recreational players.

title: Changes in the Game Characteristics of a Badminton Match: A Longitudinal Study through the Olympic Game Finals Analysis in Men's Singles
author: Laffaye G, Phomsoupha M, Dor F
publisher: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 14:584-590
notes: Olympic MS finals 1992-2012: rest time rose 14.8 to 33.5 s; rally ~10 s; shot frequency up ~34%. Authors recommend metabolic training at ~1:3 work:rest with high-intensity rallies, developing both aerobic and alactic systems. Elite-only, observational.

title: A comparison of singles and doubles badminton: heart rate response, player profiles and game characteristics
author: Alcock A, Cable NT
publisher: International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 9(2):228-237
notes: Singles mean/peak HR 88.8%/96.8% HRmax vs doubles 75.5%/89.0%; singles ~594 steps/game vs ~315; singles players higher predicted VO2max (50.6 vs 45.5). Abstract only.

title: Notational singles match analysis of male badminton players who participated in the African Badminton Championships
author: Abdullahi Y, Coetzee B
publisher: International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport (post-print, Ahmadu Bello University repository)
notes: 20 men's singles matches: per match ~46 forward lunges, ~52 half-lunges, ~175 chasse steps, ~62 split-steps, ~38 scissor kicks; 68 rallies, 6.5 shots/rally; real playing time 29.8% of match.

title: European singles and doubles badminton matches analysis with specific focus on pair doubles
author: Le Mansec Y, Boiveau M, Doron J, Jubeau M
publisher: International Journal of Racket Sports Science 5(1):14-22
notes: Singles ~40% more jumps and ~250% more lunges than doubles; men's/mixed doubles rallies ~45% shorter, rests ~18% longer. Abstract only (relative values).

title: Oxygen cost and physiological responses of recreational badminton match play
author: Deka P, Berg K, Harder J, Batelaan H, McGrath M
publisher: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness 57(6):760-765
notes: 14 recreational men (~36 y), 30-min singles: VO2 76% of max, mean HR 168 bpm; HR higher in last 10 min; RPE rose 15.8 to 17.6 from 15 to 30 min; ~2,400 steps; ~392 kcal. Vigorous intensity. Amateur evidence.

title: The relationship between aerobic fitness and recovery from high intensity intermittent exercise
author: Tomlin DL, Wenger HA
notes: Aerobic fitness linked to faster PCr regeneration and better power recovery across repeated efforts; lactate-removal evidence mixed. Abstract read via Europe PMC.

title: Anaerobic and Aerobic Energy System Contribution During Maximal Exercise: A Systematic Review
author: Gastin PB, Suppiah HT
notes: 102 studies: anaerobic energy dominates single maximal efforts up to ~75-80 s; equal contribution at ~79 s; systems work together dynamically. Abstract read via Europe PMC. Supports 'all engines run at once' analogy.

title: High-intensity interval training, solutions to the programming puzzle: Part I: cardiopulmonary emphasis
author: Buchheit M, Laursen PB
notes: HIT = repeated short-to-long high-intensity bouts with recovery; repeated sprints/all-out efforts effective for team and racket-sport players; aim for several minutes per session at >=90% VO2max; nine programming variables. Abstract only.

title: Effects of physical training programs on healthy badminton players' performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis
author: Ma S, Xue W, Soh KG, et al.
publisher: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation 17:189
notes: 15 studies, 370 players, 4-10 wk, 2-3 sessions/wk. HIIT and sprint interval training improved VO2max (SMD 1.27, but only 2 studies/32 players); strength/plyometric/core improve agility. Small samples, unclear blinding. Full text via Europe PMC PMC12239426.

title: Effects of resistance training on performance in competitive badminton players: a systematic review
author: Wang T, Ng YG, Amri S, Kamalden TF, Gao Z
notes: 14 studies, 377 players: resistance training improved power, speed, agility and endurance; lower-limb training clearest for jumps; typical 2-3 sessions/wk for 4-14 wk. Small, mostly male samples.

title: Quantity and quality of exercise for developing and maintaining cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal, and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy adults (ACSM Position Stand) — reviewed in 'From 1998 to 2011: ACSM Publishes Updated Exercise Guidelines'
author: Garber CE et al. (position stand); summary by Kravitz L
publisher: Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 43(7):1334-1359 / University of New Mexico
notes: Cardio: >=3 d/wk vigorous (RPE 14-17) 20-60 min or >=5 d/wk moderate (RPE 12-13) 30-60 min; progress gradually. Resistance: 2-3 d/wk, 48 h between same muscles, 60-70% 1RM for novice-intermediate, 8-12 reps, 2-4 sets, 2-3 min rest. Flexibility-injury link not substantiated. Read via faithful summary tables, not original.

title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
author: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB
notes: 25 RCTs, 26,610 participants: strength training RR 0.315 (injuries cut to <1/3); proprioception RR 0.55; multi-component RR 0.655; stretching RR 0.963 (no effect). Abstract via Europe PMC. Not badminton-specific.

title: The effect of plyometric training volume on jumping performance
author: Ebben WP, Suchomel TJ, Garceau LR
notes: Cites recommendations of 80-100 foot contacts/session for novices (Potach & Chu 2008; Chu & Myer 2013); low-volume (60-100 contacts, 2x/wk, 48-96 h apart) as effective as double volume. Year approximate: not printed on the PDF.

title: Systematic review on badminton injuries: incidence, characteristics and risk factors
author: Stepper B, Hecksteden A, Stagge H, Faude O, Donath L
notes: 19 studies: ~1-4 injuries per 1,000 h; lower body 41-92% of injuries; strains, sprains, tendinopathy, stress fractures; 73-100% mild/moderate. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Acute Achilles tendon rupture in badminton players
author: Fahlstrom M, Bjornstig U, Lorentzon R
notes: 31 ruptures, mean age 36; 97% recreational/beginners; 94% at the middle or end of a game; 16% had earlier local symptoms. Authors suggest local fatigue may play a role; recommend strength, endurance and coordination training and early care of minor injuries.

title: Adjusted Landing Technique Reduces the Load on the Achilles Tendon in Badminton Players
author: Kaldau NC, Nedergaard NJ, Holmich P, Bencke J
publisher: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 21:224-232
notes: Danish data: 21% of Achilles ruptures occurred in badminton; risk among recreational men 31-45; landing on externally rotated non-racket foot (with upper-body rotation) cut estimated Achilles force ~25% (68 to 50 N/kg). Lab study, n=20.

title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance (Joint Position Statement)
author: American College of Sports Medicine, American Dietetic Association, Dietitians of Canada (Rodriguez NR, DiMarco NM, Langley S)
notes: Dehydration >2-3% body mass decreases performance; don't drink in excess of sweat rate; during exercise ~30-60 g carbohydrate/h, especially for sessions >1 h; carbohydrate/electrolyte drinks help. DOI 10.1249/MSS.0b013e318190eb86.

title: Laws of Badminton — Law 16 Continuous play, misconduct and penalties (copy hosted by Tower Hamlets Council)
author: Badminton World Federation
notes: Law 16.2: intervals not exceeding 60 s when leading score reaches 11, and not exceeding 120 s between games. Applies to 3x21 scoring; secondary copy of BWF text.

title: BWF Approves 3x15 Scoring System
author: USA Badminton
notes: BWF members adopted 3x15 scoring at the 87th AGM (April 2026), effective 4 January 2027. Interval details not given on this page.

title: Intensity of tennis match play
author: Fernandez J, Mendez-Villanueva A, Pluim BM
notes: Tennis alternates maximal/near-maximal bursts with moderate/low intensity; matches often >1 h, sometimes >5 h. Abstract only (via Europe PMC); used only for sport-variation contrast.

title: Interaction among Skeletal Muscle Metabolic Energy Systems during Intense Exercise
author: Baker JS, McCormick MC, Robergs RA
notes: Phosphagen system dominates maximal efforts of ~5–6 s; CrP largely depleted within ~10 s; all three systems contribute at once (added by fact-checker).

title: Aerobic high-intensity intervals improve VO2max more than moderate training
author: Helgerud J, et al.
notes: 40 moderately trained men, 8 wk, 3x/wk; 4x4 min at 90–95% HRmax and 15s/15s intervals both improved VO2max more than steady training. Running, not badminton (added by fact-checker).

title: Achilles tendon rupture — patient information leaflet (AAE_ATR_02)
author: St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
notes: Patients feel as if someone has hit them on the back of the heel, often with a snapping or popping sound, and find it difficult to walk or stand on tip toe. Generic red-flag line only (replaces CUH page per second-pass fact-check).
